title: Left Half Pyramid
description: Brute force to optimized: per-cell space-or-star checks versus building the gap and star regions directly, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print a right aligned triangle of stars with n rows, where row i contains n minus i leading spaces followed by i stars, so every row ends flush against the same right edge.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Triangle Leaning Against the Right Wall
blocks.text: Picture the same growing rows of bricks as a plain pyramid, except this time every row is pushed all the way to the right, against a wall. The shorter rows need padding on the left to reach that wall, and as the rows get longer, less padding is needed, until the last row needs none at all.

blocks.caption: Row i is n minus i spaces followed by exactly i stars

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row","Output","Why"],"rows":[["Row 1","   *","3 leading spaces, n minus i, followed by 1 star, i."],["Row 2","  **","2 leading spaces followed by 2 stars."],["Row 3"," ***","1 leading space followed by 3 stars."],["Row 4","****","0 leading spaces followed by 4 stars, flush against the right edge."]]}

blocks.text: No rows at all, so nothing is printed.
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what is actually being decided at each position.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Unlike the plain left aligned pyramid, each row here has two distinct parts, a leading gap of spaces and a trailing region of stars.

Observation 2: The size of both parts is fully determined by the row number before the row is even started, row i always needs exactly n minus i spaces and exactly i stars.

Observation 3: Checking each of the n column positions individually to decide space or star repeats the same, already-known split point over and over, once per column, when that split point never actually changes within a row.

Observation 4: Since both region sizes are known in advance, each region can be built directly in one operation and simply concatenated together, with no per cell decision needed at all.
That reasoning alone already replaces per-column checking with direct construction of two known-size regions.

Use an outer loop for each row i, and an inner loop that checks every one of the n column positions, deciding for each one individually whether it still falls inside the leading gap or has reached the star region.

items: Loop over each row i from 1 to n.
Inside that, check every one of the n column positions.
If the position is still within the first n minus i columns, print a space.
Otherwise, print a star.
After finishing a row, move to the next line.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check every column position and decide space or star

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The inner loop checks all n column positions individually, deliberately mirroring a naive character-by-character rendering where each position's identity, space or star, gets decided fresh every time.
The comparison against the split point n minus i is recomputed on every single column check, even though that split point never changes across all n checks within the same row.
Printing happens immediately inside the inner loop, one character at a time, rather than assembling the row first, which is exactly the per-cell overhead the next section removes.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every column position in every row is individually checked and assigned the right character.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since all n columns are checked in every one of the n rows.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: checking every column position one at a time, even though the split point between spaces and stars is already known in advance for each row, wastes a per cell decision that never actually changes within a row. The exact count of spaces and stars for row i is already known before the row even starts, so both regions can be built directly in one operation each, with no per cell checking at all.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column works but is wasteful: the split point between spaces and stars, n minus i, is exactly the same for every single column check within a row, yet it gets re-evaluated n times per row anyway.

What is already known before the row starts: both region sizes, n minus i spaces and i stars, are fully determined the moment row i begins.

Can both regions be built without checking individual positions: yes, a direct repeat operation builds a region of any known size in one step, with no per-position decision needed.

What happens once both regions exist: they are simply concatenated together, in order, to form the complete row.

The core idea: build the space region and the star region directly, using their already-known sizes, then concatenate them into one row.

For each row i, build the leading gap and the star region directly, using one operation for the n minus i spaces and another for the i stars, then concatenate them into a single row string. This removes all per cell branching, needing only one print call per row.
For each row i, build both regions directly using their known sizes, then concatenate and print.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: build the spaces and stars directly, one print call per row

blocks.text: This works because a row's two regions, the leading gap and the star region, have sizes that are both simple, known functions of the row number, n minus i and i respectively, so directly repeating a space character n minus i times and a star character i times, then concatenating the two results, produces exactly the same row that checking every column individually would have produced, just without ever making a per-position decision. Since the two region sizes always add up to exactly n, the concatenated row is always exactly n characters wide, matching every other row.

items: The space region and star region are each built with their own direct repeat operation, one call for n minus i spaces, one call for i stars, rather than any loop deciding between them position by position.
The two regions are concatenated in a single expression, spaces first then stars, which is what determines the correct left to right ordering of the finished row.
No comparison or branching survives into this version at all, both region sizes are simply used directly as repeat counts.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, since that is the size of the output, but with no per cell branching and only O(n) print calls instead of O(n squared) checks.
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly in one operation, so instead of printing each one separately, all n rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

items: Every row is still built from its own two directly constructed regions, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is deferring output until every row exists.
Joining all n rows with newline characters assembles the complete multi-line pattern as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole triangle, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: Whenever a row can be split into clearly defined regions, like a leading gap and a star region here, checking each position individually is unnecessary once the exact size of every region is known in advance. Building each region directly and concatenating them is both simpler to reason about and far cheaper in terms of output operations.

items: Swapping the space and star counts, using i spaces and n minus i stars instead of the other way around.
Off by one errors in the gap size, since row i needs exactly n minus i spaces, not n minus i plus one or n minus i minus one.
Forgetting the n = 0 edge case, where nothing at all should be printed.

blocks.text: Right aligned patterns like this one are the natural next step after a plain left aligned pyramid, and the same space count plus star count formula reused here shows up again, with small variations, in diamonds, hourglasses, and butterfly patterns later on.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every column", think: both region sizes, spaces and stars, are known before the row starts, build them directly.
If the interviewer says "how do the two regions combine", think: simple concatenation, spaces first, then stars, since their sizes always sum to n.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build every row first, join with newlines, print once.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: per cell checks in the brute force version, one formula built row per print call in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: pattern printing with two distinct, known-size regions per row, a leading gap and a star region, built directly instead of decided cell by cell.

Core Idea: row i always needs exactly n minus i spaces and i stars, both known before the row starts, so each region is built with its own direct repeat operation and simply concatenated, then every row can be batched into a single output call.
Time: O(n squared) checks and calls for the brute force, O(n) calls for the optimized version, O(1) call for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: once a row's regions have known, fixed sizes, per-position checking is pure overhead, direct construction and concatenation always suffice.
Interview Difficulty: easy to get the shape right with per-cell checks; recognizing and eliminating the redundant per-column decision is what shows real efficiency awareness.
One line memory trick: build the gap and the stars directly from their known sizes, concatenate, then batch into one output call.
